title: Podcast with Steve Gibson, President of Americas at JIJ - Quantum Computing Report
gist: JIJ's Americas president Steve Gibson says ~80% of its commercial optimization work runs on classical or quantum-inspired solvers, defines today's 'advantage' as a better (not faster) answer via problem decomposition, sees hardware roadmaps converging on 2029-2031, and is using AI to shift JIJ from services toward scalable software.

themes.theme: Where quantum optimization actually runs today

insights.claim: About 80% of JIJ's commercial optimization engagements end up on classical or quantum-inspired solvers, with only about 20% using traditional quantum hardware.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Revenue at quantum software firms today is largely classical; investors should not equate 'quantum company' revenue with quantum-hardware demand.
insights.quote: I would say around about 80% of the more commercial engagements end up sitting in the classical or quantum-inspired space, and then 20% is in that more traditional quantum space

insights.claim: JIJ's customers are mostly in Japan, including recent announcements with Kobelco in manufacturing logistics, plus European work in energy and finance.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Japanese industrial customers are an underappreciated source of quantum-optimization demand.
insights.locator: Yeah, so we have a number of customers.

insights.claim: Gibson defines advantage pragmatically as improving on what is done today, rather than formal quantum advantage claims.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Vendors using loose definitions of 'advantage' means investors must scrutinize benchmark claims.
insights.quote: The way I look at advantage is, have I improved something versus what is being done today?
insights.locator: So I see where you’re going

insights.claim: In a UK national program, JIJ decomposed a problem to run partly on a quantum photonic system; it was not faster than the best classical method but produced a slightly better answer.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Evidence of marginal quality gains, not speedups — a modest proof point for hybrid approaches.
insights.quote: It wasn’t faster, but it got a better overall answer.
insights.locator: It wasn’t faster, but it got

insights.claim: When the best classical approach was applied, monolithic classical solving outperformed classical solving of the decomposed problem, yet the quantum decomposition approach slightly eked out on performance.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Shows problem formulation choices can dominate hardware choice in benchmark results.
insights.quote: the classical worked better doing it monolithically than it did on the decomposition. But the decomposition approach ended up slightly eking out on performance

insights.claim: Gibson argues that as GPUs become more performant, it will be harder and harder to prove quantum advantage in optimization.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: A rising classical/GPU bar is a headwind for quantum optimization pure-plays and a tailwind for GPU incumbents.
insights.quote: As GPUs become more performant, it’s going to be harder and harder to prove that quantum advantage in the optimization space.

insights.claim: Quantum processors should be treated as co-processors for the hardest combinatorial sub-problems rather than a rip-and-replace for classical computing, just as CPUs persist alongside GPUs.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Supports a hybrid HPC-QPU market structure where classical incumbents remain central.
insights.quote: It’s going to remain as a co-processor. No different than we still use CPUs even though GPUs are around.
insights.locator: So everything’s going to be a case-by-case

insights.claim: Problem formulation and decomposition matter as much as hardware: huge complex problems must be broken down even for classical systems, making software engineering and constraint understanding central.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Value may accrue to formulation/software layers rather than to hardware alone.
insights.locator: Am I decomposing it down into sub-problems?

insights.claim: Gibson notes quantum computing has been 'five years away' for the six years he has been in the industry.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: A reminder that quantum timelines have repeatedly slipped.
insights.quote: I’ve been in it for six years, and it’s been five years away for those six years, right?

insights.claim: Hardware providers are coalescing around a 2029-2031 timeframe and many appear to be hitting milestones, leading Gibson to call quantum's arrival an inevitability rather than a question of if.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Industry consensus on 2029-2031 sets a window for when commercial expectations — and valuations — will be tested.
insights.quote: they are all kind of coalescing around the same 2029 through 2031 timeframe, and a lot of them seem to be hitting the milestones pretty well
insights.locator: That being said, each of the computers

insights.claim: Organizations should prepare now because business readiness — data compliance, legal sign-off, new data structures and transfers — can take years, beyond just technical pilots.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Readiness consulting and enterprise preparation spend can precede hardware maturity.
insights.quote: It’s not just the technical aspects, but it’s also the actual business readiness.
insights.locator: And so I would say it is an inevitability.

insights.claim: Gibson compares quantum preparedness to the ChatGPT moment in AI, arguing companies unprepared then are still behind the curve.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Frames FOMO-driven enterprise adoption as a demand driver for quantum services.
insights.quote: No different than the ChatGPT moment happened in AI, and those companies that were not ready are still behind the curve, right?
insights.locator: What I would say is, definitely

insights.claim: Commercial accessibility has changed greatly in six years, with platforms like Amazon Braket making many machines easily accessible.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Cloud hyperscalers have become key distribution channels for quantum hardware.
insights.locator: What I will say is when I started

themes.theme: AI-enabled shift from services to software

insights.claim: JIJ started as a services company and is using AI to let customers describe problems in their own terms, aiming to transition toward a scalable software product model.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Productization would improve margins and scalability versus consulting-heavy quantum software models.
insights.quote: Our goal is to be a software company
insights.locator: And so now by doing that

insights.claim: Approachability is one of the biggest customer barriers; previously every domain needed an engineer to translate business terms into optimization formulations, which AI can now automate.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: AI could lower the expertise barrier and expand the addressable customer base for quantum software.
insights.quote: One of the biggest barriers for most customers is approachability.

insights.claim: JIJ builds a repository of knowledge and approaches from customer engagements (not customer data) to upskill its AI agents.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Engagement-derived know-how could become a proprietary data moat.
insights.locator: My hope is that AI allows

insights.claim: JIJ is piloting a 'center of excellence' engagement model combining education and application to upskill client teams, alongside discovery-then-POC engagements.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Indicates continued services revenue mix in the near term.

insights.claim: Over 60% of JIJ's staff are technical, and its founders came from Professor Nishimori's lab, regarded as the father of annealing; the name derives from the Ising model.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Deep Japanese research talent is JIJ's differentiation as it expands to U.S. and EU.
insights.locator: From my perspective, I want to get closer

insights.claim: JIJ wants closer research collaborations with U.S. hardware companies and system integrators as it expands beyond Japan.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Possible partnership announcements with U.S. hardware vendors.
insights.locator: From my perspective, I want to get closer
